subject: Chemistry
title: Microplastics: Chemistry That Won't Disappear
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Microplastics: Chemistry That Won't Disappear.

hook.text: Microplastics have been found in human blood, lungs, placentas, and breast milk. They are now inside every living person.

buildup.text: Plastics don't biodegrade—they photodegrade. UV light breaks them into smaller pieces, but the polymers persist.

discovery.text: Particles under 5 mm are called microplastics. Under 1 μm, they're nanoplastics—small enough to enter cells.

twist.text: You ingest about 5 grams of microplastic per week—roughly the weight of a credit card. Most comes from water and food packaging.

climax.text: We produce 400 million tons of plastic yearly. Less than 9% is recycled. The rest accumulates in oceans, soil, and bodies.

punchline.text: Polymers that last centuries, fragments that enter cells. Chemistry's most durable error.

quiz.question: Why are microplastics so persistent in the environment?
options: Plastics photodegrade into smaller pieces but the polymer chains don't biodegrade
Bacteria cannot survive on plastic surfaces to break them down
Microplastics are too heavy to be carried away by water

details.summary: Microplastics are synthetic polymer fragments smaller than five millimeters that result from the breakdown of larger plastic waste or are manufactured for products like cosmetics. They now contaminate every ocean, most drinking water supplies, and have been found in human blood and lung tissue.
details.whyItMatters: Microplastics represent a novel chemical pollution crisis with unknown long-term health effects. Their persistence and ubiquity make them one of the defining environmental challenges of the twenty-first century.
takeaways: Microplastics are now found in oceans, tap water, and human blood
Plastics take hundreds of years to degrade and never fully disappear
They absorb and concentrate other toxic chemicals from the environment

faq.question: How do microplastics enter the human body?
faq.answer: Humans ingest microplastics through drinking water, seafood, salt, and food packaged in plastic. We also inhale airborne microplastic fibers from synthetic clothing and carpets. Studies estimate people consume roughly a credit card's worth of plastic weekly, though effects are still being studied.

faq.question: Can microplastics be removed from the environment?
faq.answer: Removal is extremely difficult at scale due to their microscopic size and widespread distribution. Water filtration can remove some particles, and emerging enzymatic degradation shows promise..
